title: Accuracy of chronic kidney disease codes in general practice records against laboratory-defined disease
subtitle: Design not yet settled: prevalence of uncoded disease or accuracy of the codes
statement: In a primary care network of six practices, chronic kidney disease registers appear too small: patients with repeatedly low eGFR results lack a kidney disease code, and some patients are coded after a single low result during acute illness. The network does not know how accurate its kidney disease codes are against laboratory-defined disease (two eGFR values below 60 at least 90 days apart), which it needs to know before deciding whether to fund a recoding exercise.
whoAffected: About 48,000 registered patients, especially older adults and people with diabetes or hypertension whose kidney disease may be uncoded; the GPs, pharmacists and nurses who run reviews; and the network's planners.
whatHurts: An uncoded patient misses annual kidney reviews, blood pressure targets and dose checks for renally cleared medicines; a wrongly coded patient carries a label, extra monitoring and sometimes withheld medicines.
currentPractice: Codes are added by clinicians during consultations or after hospital letters; no routine search compares codes with laboratory results across the network.
whyNow: A pharmacist's search in one practice found both missed and doubtful codes, and the network decides on a recoding exercise in March 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Every patient whose kidney function is persistently reduced is known to the practice and reviewed, and nobody carries a kidney disease label from a single low result.
summary: Problem framed; the design is left open (prevalence of uncoded disease or accuracy of the codes); the reply returns no constraints of its own.
